rationale: Differences 2,4,6,8 follow one familiar growing-difference rule; take the differences once, extend once.
The first differences (3,2,5,7) do not suggest a rule, so the candidate has to abandon the default method and discover that each term is the sum of the previous two.
Two interleaved strands each move by a constant 3. Splitting the sequence is the only idea and it is routine for this cohort.
Differences 3,6,9,12 are the multiples of three; one level of differences and an obvious pattern.
First differences 2,6,10,14 are not constant, so a second level of differences (constant 4) must be found before extending.

Two interleaved strands with different steps (+3 and -4) and a position trap: the next term belongs to the first strand, and the other strand's next value (38) is offered as a distractor. Borderline easy.
Additive recurrence (each term is the sum of the previous two). Visible from 3+4=7, but it is a non-linear idea that most Year 6 candidates have not met. Borderline easy.
No rule is stated. The candidate must hypothesise and test an invariant (every row and column sums to 30) before the missing cell can be found.
Heads-and-legs needs an assume-all-chickens correction or a systematic trial with two coupled constraints; a classic but not a one-step item.
Five consecutive numbers: the middle term is the mean (27), so the largest is 29. One shortcut, one step.
Halve the perimeter, then solve a sum-and-difference pair and report the length rather than the width. Short, but three linked steps. Borderline easy.
Two coordinated constraints on the digits plus a quotient-and-remainder condition; the candidate has to build N = 7(t+u)+3 with t = u+3 and solve. Clearly the hardest item in the section.
One unknown with direct relationships (M + M+4 + 2M = 44). The label is right; the estimator over-reads its word count.
A short factor-pair search for sum 18 and product 72, then the difference. Borderline easy because the pair is found quickly.
Three sequential signed changes with direction words. Several operations but one idea, so easy.
A double negative inside a four-term expression; the sign handling, not the arithmetic, is the demand.
Percentage difference (20%) of a total, or two simple percentages. Routine.
Percentage increase on friendly numbers. The wrong-base trap (20%) is well known and is offered as a distractor.
Share $72,000 in the ratio 2:3:4 and report the middle share. Standard.
Ratio parts of a total with friendly numbers.
Sum and difference of two ages with small numbers.
Unknown on both sides of a given equation. Procedural, but collecting terms across the equals sign is above routine Year 6 work.
Three consecutive odd numbers need either the mean shortcut (29, then +2) or x, x+2, x+4 set up and solved. The distractor 29 catches the slip. Borderline easy.
Two linear conditions in two unknowns, solved by substitution or elimination. Arguably the hardest maths item in this group and could be argued up to challenging.
Direct substitution; the only care needed is reading 2qr as a product and applying order of operations.
A verbal description must be translated into 6n - 14 = 2n + 18, then solved with the unknown on both sides.
Vertically opposite angles are equal, then an unknown-on-both-sides solve, then back-substitution to report the angle rather than x.
All three angles must be expressed through one variable and summed to 180; the distractor 40 is the value of B, not A.
Supplementary angles plus a careful translation of '36 less than three times'; the question asks for the smaller angle, so the other angle must be checked.
Subtract one square area from another.
Needs the polygon angle-sum rule or the exterior-angle idea, which is stretch content for Year 6; the arithmetic after that is easy.
Complement probability as a percentage; the NOT in the stem is the only trap.
Inclusion-exclusion (or a Venn diagram) to avoid double-counting the 7 who play both sports.
A repeated change followed by one more; the result crosses zero but the arithmetic is two simple steps.
Build a perimeter expression that counts the repeated side twice, collect terms, then solve for k.
